user_query: What did DRCR.net Protocol T compare in diabetic retinopathy / DME research?
draft_answer: DRCR.net Protocol T was a pivotal study that compared the efficacy of three anti-VEGF agents—aflibercept, bevacizumab, and ranibizumab—in the treatment of diabetic macular edema (DME). This randomized trial aimed to evaluate the visual outcomes and safety profiles of these drugs when used as monotherapy for DME. The study provided critical insights into the relative effectiveness of these treatments, influencing clinical decision-making in managing DME [4]. The trial's findings were significant in establishing aflibercept as a preferred option in certain cases due to its superior visual acuity outcomes in patients with worse baseline vision [4].

chunks.document_name: pubmed_42920596_PMC13690659_Mapping the methodological framework of diabetic retinopathy.pdf
chunks.document_content: Allocation Anti-VEGF combined with retinal laser photocoagulation ac-counted for 45.65% of the main combination regimens. Anti-VEGF drugs (e.g., ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab) rapidly reduce macular edema and inhibit neovascular activity by neutralizing VEGF, with a fast onset but limited duration of action. Laser photocoagulation, by contrast, destroys high oxygen-consuming photoreceptor cells to reduce retinal ischemia and hypoxia, thereby decreasing sustained VEGF production; it offers durable efficacy but a slower onset. Seminal trials, including the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) and DRCR.net Protocol I, have established the evidence base for current management strat-egies: ETDRS defined diagnostic criteria and laser standards, while Protocol I validated combination therapy efficacy. Anti-VEGF combined with glucocorticoids may benefit patients who respond poorly to anti-VEGF therapy alone, but the adverse effects such as increased intraocular pressure and accelerated cataract progression limit their widespread use. The current main treatment regimen for CI-DME/PDR is centered on anti-VEGF therapy, with individual-ized plans optimized based on patient-specific conditions. Future research should focus on optimizing combination regimen timing, identifying suitable patient populations, the exploration of novel combination strategies (34). The sample sizes of diabetic retinopathy studies are generally small - 61.81% enrolled fewer than 100 participants, with studies of 1-50 participants being the most common (39.18%), while large-scale trials with over 300 participants accounted for only 13.15%. This scarcity of adequately powered studies is partly attributable to the relatively small PDR patient pool at individual centers, making it difficult for single sites to accrue more than 100 cases (36). Small samples compromise statistical power and increase the risk of type II errors, thereby undermining both internal validity and reproduc-ibility of reported treatment effects. The establishment of multicen-ter collaborative networks, such as the DRCR.net series (Protocol I/ T/V), RESTORE, RESOLVE, and VISTA/VIVID, is therefore es-sential not only to increase enrollment capacity but also to ensure sufficient power for detecting clinically meaningful effects and to enhance the generalizability of findings across diverse populations (37). Future trials should prespecify minimum sample size calcula-tions based on clinically relevant effect sizes and incorporate interim power analyses where appropriate. Age standards are primarily focused on adults, consistent with normal research patterns. Gender standards did not impose restrictions, reflecting good awareness of external validity. Only one study was limited to males. Overall, reporting on the gender dimension is relatively standardized, but subsequent analyses should still pay attention to efficacy differences in gender subgroups. Baseline CRT values in women are usually lower than in men, which may affect the diagnostic threshold for DME and the assessment of treatment response. The United States demonstrated a strong emphasis on anti-VEGF therapies, with a total of 69 studies (47 trial registrations and 22 publications) indexed in PubMed. In contrast, China showed a predominant focus on perioperative interventions, with a total of 40 studies (35 trial registrations and 5 publications in PubMed). These findings suggest that geographical regions may have specific prior-ities in therapeutic strategies, accompanied by varying rates of translation from registration to publication. Intervention timing is mostly individualized, often without fixed treatment numbers and frequencies.

chunks.document_content: The role of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR/ErbB1) in diabetic retinopathy and its therapeutic implications Clinically, DM is classified into at least four categories, namely Type 1 (T1DM), Type 2 (T2DM), gestational diabetes, and other types arising from specific identi­ fiable causes [1]. In T1DM, an autoimmune response destroys insulin-producing β-cells in the pancreas, lead­ ing to an absolute insulin deficiency [1, 2]. In contrast, T2DM begins with insulin resistance of primarily skeletal muscle, adipose tissue, and the liver, followed by a pro­ gressive, nonautoimmune decline in pancreatic β-cell function and insulin secretion [1]. Uncontrolled chronic hyperglycemia in both T1DM and T2DM can lead to a range of macrovascular and microvascular complications including cardiovascular [3], renal [4], neuronal [5], and retinal pathologies [6]. In addition to chronic hyperglyce­ mia, the classical risk factors for diabetes complications include smoking, dyslipidemias and hypertension [7]. to chronic retinal ischemia which results in prolifera­ tive diabetic retinopathy (PDR) [18]. At this stage, visual alterations are significantly more pronounced where damage to the retinal blood vessels is more severe, stimu­ lating the growth of new abnormal blood vessels (neovas­ cularization) through the process of angiogenesis [18]. This occurs through the upregulation of growth factors such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), both of which are expressed in response to hypoxia and are known to pro­ mote neovascularization [19, 20]. Additionally, diabetic macular edema (DME) is a common complication of both NPDR and PDR, where the blood-retinal-barrier (BRB) is compromised with increased vascular permeability cul­ minating in fluid accumulation in the macula, the central region of the retina responsible for sharp, detailed vision [14]. DME is a common cause of visual impairment in DR patients [18]. ​Introduction Diabetes Mellitus (DM) is a group of chronic endocrine diseases characterized by persistent hyperglycemia [1]. The current standard of care for DR centers on intra­ vitreal anti-VEGF therapy, with agents such as bevaci­ zumab, a monoclonal antibody targeting VEGF-A [21]. Among various other inflammatory mediators, VEGF plays a central role in promoting both neovasculariza­ tion and vascular leakage in PDR [20]. Under hyperglyce­ mic and hypoxic conditions, hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α) upregulates VEGF expression which drives angiogenesis via ligand binding and downstream sig­ naling [22]. By sequestering VEGF and/or inhibiting its receptor signaling, these agents decrease fluid extravasa­ tion, resolve edema, and inhibit angiogenesis associated with PDR in the optic disc, retina and iris [23]. This review focuses on diabetic retinopathy (DR), the primary microvascular complication of diabetes and a leading cause of new cases of blindness among adults aged 20-74 years in developed countries [6, 7]. Approxi­ mately one-third of individuals with diabetes develop DR [8]. Its prevalence correlates strongly with both disease duration and glycemic control, as maintaining near-nor­ moglycemia can delay or prevent its onset and progres­ sion [7]. However, recent studies have also suggested that intensive therapies that result in rapid reductions in Hemoglobin A1C (HbA1C), such as with glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists, can be associated with initial worsening of DR at least in the early stages but may ultimately be protective in late or advanced stages [9-12].

chunks.document_content: Introduction new therapeutic targets and developing more effica­ cious treatment strategies have become particularly urgent. Diabetic Retinopathy (DR), as one of the most com­ mon microvascular complications of diabetes, affects approximately 34.6% of individuals living with dia­ betes, with 30% progressing to varying degrees of vis­ ual impairment (Wang et al., 2024). The pathological characteristics primarily include capillary degener­ ation, loss of pericytes, and vessel leakage (Liu et al., 2023). At present, the therapeutic strategies for DR mainly focus on systemic treatment, vitrectomy, ret­ inal photocoagulation, and intravitreal injection of anti-VEGF inhibitors (Yamato et al., 2024). While these treatments primarily address advanced DR, their efficacy is limited for early-stage disease. They can also result in many adverse reactions, including pos­ sible permanent loss of peripheral vision and worsen­ ing macular edema (Hu et al., 2024). Thus, exploring As intrinsic resident immune cells of the retina, microglia maintain homeostatic distribution under physiological conditions and participate in the dynamic equilibrium of the retinal microenvironment by constantly surveilling the local microenvironment, clearing metabolic waste, and stabilizing synaptic structures (Guo et al., 2022). Exposure to high glucose and oxidative stress triggers reactive activation of ret­ inal microglia, accompanied by enhanced secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-1b, IL-6, and TNF-a. chunks.document_content: Published: October 16, 2026 The level of Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) is commonly used to characterize ocular microvascular complications of diabetes, the leading cause of preventable blindness amongst working-aged people [1]. Shorter durations of diabetes, improved glycemic control, and lower blood pressure and lipid levels are implicated in reducing the risk for development and progression of DR [2]. A review of prior research [3] identified studies focused on prevalence, incidence and progression of DR and the risk factors associated with them. However, regression (or improvement) of DR is less frequently studied or is a secondary focus. Data availability statement: The minimal data set is available at Harvard Dataverse via https:// doi.org/10.7910/DVN/Q5HFML. Funding: The author(s) received no specific funding for this work. Dara Shahon: Employee of the Indian Health Service as Director, IHS-JVN Teleophthalmology Program at the Phoenix Indian Medical Center. Available studies on regression (Table 1) suggest it is more likely to occur in very mild nonproliferative DR (NPDR) [6,19], particularly for younger patients with hemo­ globin A1c (HbA1c) levels close to normal and shorter diabetes duration [11,13,16]. Generally, the literature addressing regression focused on improvements in risk factors known to be associated with progression of DR. However, one publication [8] suggested that the formation of microaneurysms (MAs), a characteristic lesion for mild NPDR, was independent of glycemic control and other medical factors that affect more advanced levels of DR. Sven-Erik Bursell: Scientific consultant for SocialEyes Corp. and Research Consultant subcontracted by the Indian Health Service Joslin Vision Network to manage and analyze the data collected for the program. Sterphanie The primary aim of this study was to investigate the occurrence of DR regression in teleophthalmology patients with initially very mild NPDR or mild NPDR. Rates of no change or stability and any progression were also determined for comparison pur­ poses. A secondary aim was to examine the association of diabetes therapy, diabetes duration, and HbA1c with regression occurrence. Prior results on this study cohort [20,21] demonstrated prevalence of any DR, any DME, and sight-threatening disease was 28.6%, 3.0%, and 3.0%. Of patients with no DR in 2015, 18.0% had mild NPDR or worse in 2016-2019, and 0.1% had PDR. chunks.document_content: Materials and methods Diabetic retinopathy (DR) has long been assessed primarily as a microangiopathy. However, recent studies have proposed the con-cept of diabetic retinal disease (DRD), which recognizes that retinal pathology involves not only the vascular system but also neural and glial cells and their interactions within the neurovascular unit (2, 3). This concept has increased interest in preclinical and early clinical signs of DRD to better understand the mechanisms and timing of disease onset (2). Both basic and clinical studies have demonstrated subtle but clear functional and structural changes in retinal neural tissue in diabetes (4-8). To analyze these early changes, we have been studying diabetic eyes at a stage before visible macular changes are detectable on fundus photographs and before the development of secondary changes associated with PDR and/or exudative fluid in DME (9, 10). However, their associations with systemic biomarkers have not yet been addressed, although diabetic complications tend to be associated not only with hyperglycemia but also with broader systemic metabolic alterations. Participants Non-invasive ocular imaging systems, such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) and OCT angiography (OCTA), can detect subtle changes at the micrometer scale and are now widely used in clinical practice. OCT enables measurement not only of the thick-ness of the neural retinal layers but also of photoreceptor outer segment (PROS) length. Length of the PROS, where visual pigments are concentrated and act as light receptors, has been reported to be reduced in eyes with diabetes than in control (10), and as a marker of photoreceptor condition in eyes at high risk of age-related macular degeneration (11, 12). The volume of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), a highly metabolic single-cell layer essential for photoreceptor maintenance, can also be measured on OCT images. Eye examinations The patients underwent ophthalmic examinations, including measurement of BCVA, intraocular pressure (IOP), and axial length, and acquisition of fundus photographs (California, Optos, Inc., MA), sectional and three-dimensional spectral-domain OCT images (Spectralis OCT, Heidelberg Engineering GmbH, Dossenheim, Germany), and 3 x 3 mm OCT angiography (OCTA) (OCT HS-100; Canon, Inc., Tokyo, Japan) images. Front. Endocrinol. 17:1961622. doi: 10.3389/fendo.XXX-XXX-XXXX Background: Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) is a prevalent and sight-threatening ocular complication of diabetes, and one of the leading causes of vision loss and blindness among the working-age population worldwide. Driven by a growing understanding of the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying DR, treatment strategies have evolved from a sole focus on glycemic control to comprehensive, multi-targeted, and multimodal therapies. This study systematically summarizes the characteristics of current clinical trials focused on DR treatment and evaluates the employed research methodologies. The aim of this review is to explore methodological trends in specific domains, with the hope that such insights may inform future efforts to optimize trial design and improve trial quality. Methods: This study followed the PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines. Clinical trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov and the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR) were retrieved. In addition, clinical trials indexed in PubMed from July 23, 2016 to July 23, 2026 were retrieved. Data from the included studies were extracted and presented in tabular form. Results: Clinical research targeting DR has expanded rapidly, reflecting a shift toward diverse interventions like anti-Vascular endothelial growth factor(anti-VEGF) drugs, laser treatments, and combined therapies. However, several methodological limitations were noted in the included studies, including the failure to specify diabetes type in over half of the cases, a predominance of small-sample trials, inconsistent reporting of intervention duration, and limited implementation of blinding due to practical constraints in ophthalmic interventions. chunks.document_content: Allocation Anti-VEGF combined with retinal laser photocoagulation ac-counted for 45.65% of the main combination regimens. Anti-VEGF drugs (e.g., ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab) rapidly reduce macular edema and inhibit neovascular activity by neutralizing VEGF, with a fast onset but limited duration of action. Laser photocoagulation, by contrast, destroys high oxygen-consuming photoreceptor cells to reduce retinal ischemia and hypoxia, thereby decreasing sustained VEGF production; it offers durable efficacy but a slower onset. Seminal trials, including the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) and DRCR.net Protocol I, have established the evidence base for current management strat-egies: ETDRS defined diagnostic criteria and laser standards, while Protocol I validated combination therapy efficacy. Anti-VEGF combined with glucocorticoids may benefit patients who respond poorly to anti-VEGF therapy alone, but the adverse effects such as increased intraocular pressure and accelerated cataract progression limit their widespread use. The current main treatment regimen for CI-DME/PDR is centered on anti-VEGF therapy, with individual-ized plans optimized based on patient-specific conditions. Future research should focus on optimizing combination regimen timing, identifying suitable patient populations, the exploration of novel combination strategies (34). The sample sizes of diabetic retinopathy studies are generally small - 61.81% enrolled fewer than 100 participants, with studies of 1-50 participants being the most common (39.18%), while large-scale trials with over 300 participants accounted for only 13.15%. This scarcity of adequately powered studies is partly attributable to the relatively small PDR patient pool at individual centers, making it difficult for single sites to accrue more than 100 cases (36). Small samples compromise statistical power and increase the risk of type II errors, thereby undermining both internal validity and reproduc-ibility of reported treatment effects. The establishment of multicen-ter collaborative networks, such as the DRCR.net series (Protocol I/ T/V), RESTORE, RESOLVE, and VISTA/VIVID, is therefore es-sential not only to increase enrollment capacity but also to ensure sufficient power for detecting clinically meaningful effects and to enhance the generalizability of findings across diverse populations (37). Future trials should prespecify minimum sample size calcula-tions based on clinically relevant effect sizes and incorporate interim power analyses where appropriate. Age standards are primarily focused on adults, consistent with normal research patterns. Gender standards did not impose restrictions, reflecting good awareness of external validity. Only one study was limited to males. Overall, reporting on the gender dimension is relatively standardized, but subsequent analyses should still pay attention to efficacy differences in gender subgroups. Baseline CRT values in women are usually lower than in men, which may affect the diagnostic threshold for DME and the assessment of treatment response. The United States demonstrated a strong emphasis on anti-VEGF therapies, with a total of 69 studies (47 trial registrations and 22 publications) indexed in PubMed. In contrast, China showed a predominant focus on perioperative interventions, with a total of 40 studies (35 trial registrations and 5 publications in PubMed). These findings suggest that geographical regions may have specific prior-ities in therapeutic strategies, accompanied by varying rates of translation from registration to publication. Intervention timing is mostly individualized, often without fixed treatment numbers and frequencies.

chunks.document_content: The role of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR/ErbB1) in diabetic retinopathy and its therapeutic implications Clinically, DM is classified into at least four categories, namely Type 1 (T1DM), Type 2 (T2DM), gestational diabetes, and other types arising from specific identi­ fiable causes [1]. In T1DM, an autoimmune response destroys insulin-producing β-cells in the pancreas, lead­ ing to an absolute insulin deficiency [1, 2]. In contrast, T2DM begins with insulin resistance of primarily skeletal muscle, adipose tissue, and the liver, followed by a pro­ gressive, nonautoimmune decline in pancreatic β-cell function and insulin secretion [1]. Uncontrolled chronic hyperglycemia in both T1DM and T2DM can lead to a range of macrovascular and microvascular complications including cardiovascular [3], renal [4], neuronal [5], and retinal pathologies [6]. In addition to chronic hyperglyce­ mia, the classical risk factors for diabetes complications include smoking, dyslipidemias and hypertension [7]. to chronic retinal ischemia which results in prolifera­ tive diabetic retinopathy (PDR) [18]. At this stage, visual alterations are significantly more pronounced where damage to the retinal blood vessels is more severe, stimu­ lating the growth of new abnormal blood vessels (neovas­ cularization) through the process of angiogenesis [18]. This occurs through the upregulation of growth factors such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), both of which are expressed in response to hypoxia and are known to pro­ mote neovascularization [19, 20]. Additionally, diabetic macular edema (DME) is a common complication of both NPDR and PDR, where the blood-retinal-barrier (BRB) is compromised with increased vascular permeability cul­ minating in fluid accumulation in the macula, the central region of the retina responsible for sharp, detailed vision [14]. DME is a common cause of visual impairment in DR patients [18]. ​Introduction Diabetes Mellitus (DM) is a group of chronic endocrine diseases characterized by persistent hyperglycemia [1]. The current standard of care for DR centers on intra­ vitreal anti-VEGF therapy, with agents such as bevaci­ zumab, a monoclonal antibody targeting VEGF-A [21]. Among various other inflammatory mediators, VEGF plays a central role in promoting both neovasculariza­ tion and vascular leakage in PDR [20]. Under hyperglyce­ mic and hypoxic conditions, hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α) upregulates VEGF expression which drives angiogenesis via ligand binding and downstream sig­ naling [22]. By sequestering VEGF and/or inhibiting its receptor signaling, these agents decrease fluid extravasa­ tion, resolve edema, and inhibit angiogenesis associated with PDR in the optic disc, retina and iris [23]. This review focuses on diabetic retinopathy (DR), the primary microvascular complication of diabetes and a leading cause of new cases of blindness among adults aged 20-74 years in developed countries [6, 7]. Approxi­ mately one-third of individuals with diabetes develop DR [8]. Its prevalence correlates strongly with both disease duration and glycemic control, as maintaining near-nor­ moglycemia can delay or prevent its onset and progres­ sion [7]. However, recent studies have also suggested that intensive therapies that result in rapid reductions in Hemoglobin A1C (HbA1C), such as with glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists, can be associated with initial worsening of DR at least in the early stages but may ultimately be protective in late or advanced stages [9-12].

While these treatments primarily address advanced DR, their efficacy is limited for early-stage disease. They can also result in many adverse reactions, including pos­ sible permanent loss of peripheral vision and worsen­ ing macular edema (Hu et al., 2024). Exposure to high glucose and oxidative stress triggers reactive activation of ret­ inal microglia, accompanied by enhanced secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-1b, IL-6, and TNF-a. Driven by a growing understanding of the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying DR, treatment strategies have evolved from a sole focus on glycemic control to comprehensive, multi-targeted, and multimodal therapies. This study systematically summarizes the characteristics of current clinical trials focused on DR treatment and evaluates the employed research methodologies. The aim of this review is to explore methodological trends in specific domains, with the hope that such insights may inform future efforts to optimize trial design and improve trial quality. Methods: This study followed the PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines. Clinical trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov and the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR) were retrieved. In addition, clinical trials indexed in PubMed from July 23, 2016 to July 23, 2026 were retrieved. Data from the included studies were extracted and presented in tabular form. Results: Clinical research targeting DR has expanded rapidly, reflecting a shift toward diverse interventions like anti-Vascular endothelial growth factor(anti-VEGF) drugs, laser treatments, and combined therapies. However, several methodological limitations were noted in the included studies, including the failure to specify diabetes type in over half of the cases, a predominance of small-sample trials, inconsistent reporting of intervention duration, and limited implementation of blinding due to practical constraints in ophthalmic interventions.
